top_choice_rationale: P003 (Kiyotaki and Moore) is a single, identifiable dynamic mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices, so temporary shocks become persistent and amplified. It is about three decades old, has been tested through later work on financial frictions and macroprudential analysis, and rests on a two-author paper, so the credit needs no contested cut. I read it as distinct from the 2022 prize on bank runs and deposit insurance, since it needs no run or intermediary failure, and the citation should say so explicitly. Its weaknesses are the weaker empirical identification of collateral channels compared with the theory, narrower reach than P002 or P001, and the omission of Gertler and Gilchrist. I rank P001 (Melitz and Helpman) second. It has the strongest record of direct testing on firm-level data and is distinct from the 2008 prize, but the Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum contributions are not credited, which leaves attribution at the edges unsettled. I rank P002 (Calvo, Taylor and Woodford) third. It is conceptually central and has the largest policy footprint, but its credit is spread over eight names, Taylor's place is unstable (Gali is a proposed substitute), the micro evidence on state-dependent pricing qualifies Calvo's mechanism, and the post-2008 and 2021-23 record is contested. All three are serious prizes on merit and close together. No award is last because each of them is a mature, identifiable achievement.
recusal_note: From the profile: I am a frequent co-author and IIES colleague of Timo Boppart, who supports P003, and of John Hassler, who supports P002. This overlap should not count as independent agreement. I have no personal or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Melitz, Helpman, Calvo, Taylor or Woodford, and none of my listed co-authors is credited in P001, P002 or P003. My macroeconomic theory field is adjacent to P003 and P002. I disclose these connections without adjudicating them.
